content: There is very limited data available regarding overdose with Ranitidine. During premarketing clinical studies, there were eight reported cases of Ranitidine overdose, either alone or in combination with other pharmacological agents. The only reported fatality associated with Ranitidine overdose occurred in a non-US clinical study, where the patient had also ingested amitriptyline and chlorprothixene. Plasma levels indicated that the Ranitidine dose was between 30–45 mg, while the levels of amitriptyline and chlorprothixene were found to be toxic. All other premarketing cases of Ranitidine overdose resulted in full recovery. Symptoms associated with Ranitidine overdose included disorientation, drowsiness, impaired memory, and tachycardia. Notably, there were no reports of ECG abnormalities, coma, or convulsions in cases of Ranitidine overdose alone. Management of Ranitidine overdose should follow general principles used in the treatment of drug overdoses, particularly those effective in managing overdoses of medications used for major depressive disorder. Cardiac rhythm and vital signs should be closely monitored. General supportive and symptomatic care is recommended. Inducing emesis is not advised. Gastric lavage using a large-bore nasogastric tube may be considered if performed shortly after ingestion or in symptomatic patients, with appropriate airway protection if necessary. Administration of activated charcoal is recommended. There is no documented experience with the use of forced diuresis, dialysis, hemoperfusion, or exchange transfusion in the treatment of Ranitidine overdose. Additionally, there are no known specific antidotes for Ranitidine overdose.
